_link.title: I can describe the cause, symptoms and consequences of UTIs and kidney disease

toLevel2.stem: What type of organism most commonly causes urinary tract infections (UTIs)?

options.text: Bacteria, typically E. coli
Viruses, typically influenza
Fungi, typically Candida
Parasites, typically tapeworm

explanations.a: Correct. UTIs are caused by bacterial infections, with E. coli being the most common bacterium responsible.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Viruses do not typically cause UTIs. UTIs are bacterial infections.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While fungal infections can occur, the most common cause of UTIs is bacteria, specifically E. coli.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Parasites do not cause UTIs. UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethra.

toLevel2.stem: Why are females more likely than males to develop a UTI?

options.text: The female urethra is shorter (4 cm) than the male urethra (20 cm), making it easier for bacteria to reach the bladder
Females produce more urine than males
Females have weaker immune systems than males
The female bladder is larger, providing more space for bacteria to grow

explanations.a: Correct. The shorter female urethra (4 cm vs 20 cm in males) means bacteria have a shorter distance to travel to reach the bladder, making women 14 times more likely to experience a UTI.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Urine volume is not the reason. The key factor is the length of the urethra.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Immune system differences are not the primary reason. Urethra length is the main anatomical factor.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Bladder size is not the determining factor; it is the shorter distance bacteria must travel through the urethra.

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following is a symptom of a urinary tract infection?

options.text: A burning pain when urinating
High blood pressure
Swelling in the legs and ankles
Loss of appetite

explanations.a: Correct. A burning pain when urinating is a classic symptom of a UTI, along with frequent urge to urinate and cloudy, smelly urine.
explanations.b: Incorrect. High blood pressure is a symptom of kidney disease, not a UTI.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Swelling (puffiness) in the legs and ankles is associated with kidney disease.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Loss of appetite is a symptom of kidney disease, not typically a UTI.

options.text: A gradual loss of kidney function over time
A sudden bacterial infection of the kidney
An allergic reaction to medications processed by the kidney
A temporary blockage of the ureter

explanations.a: Correct. Chronic kidney disease is a progressive loss of nephron function over time, which can eventually require dialysis or transplant.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A sudden infection would be acute, not chronic. Chronic kidney disease develops gradually.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While medications can affect kidneys, chronic kidney disease is a progressive loss of function, not an allergic reaction.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A ureter blockage is a different condition. Chronic kidney disease involves loss of nephron function.

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following is a risk factor for chronic kidney disease?

options.text: Having diabetes
Drinking too much water
Having a short urethra
Regular exercise

explanations.a: Correct. Diabetes is a major risk factor for chronic kidney disease, along with high blood pressure, family history and age over 60.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Drinking water does not cause kidney disease. In fact, adequate hydration supports kidney function.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A short urethra is a risk factor for UTIs, not chronic kidney disease.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Regular exercise is generally protective of health and is not a risk factor for kidney disease.

toLevel2.stem: Bacteria responsible for UTIs usually enter the urinary tract through the urethra.

distractor.explanation: This is true. Bacteria, mainly E. coli, typically enter through the urethra and can travel upward to the bladder.

toLevel2.stem: Kidney disease symptoms usually appear early, when only 10% of kidney function has been lost.

distractor.explanation: Kidney disease is often called a 'silent disease' because up to 90% of kidney function can be lost before symptoms appear. This is why it is so dangerous.

toLevel2.stem: UTIs are most commonly caused by the bacterium {{blank:1}}, which enters the urinary tract through the {{blank:2}}.
The female urethra is approximately {{blank:1}} cm long, while the male urethra is approximately {{blank:2}} cm long.
A sudden loss of kidney function is called {{blank:1}} kidney failure, while a gradual loss is called {{blank:2}} kidney failure.

toLevel3.stem: Why is kidney disease often called a 'silent disease'?

options.text: Because up to 90% of kidney function can be lost before symptoms appear, as remaining nephrons compensate by working harder
Because the kidneys are located deep in the body where pain cannot be felt
Because kidney disease only affects elderly people who may not notice symptoms
Because the disease has no symptoms at any stage

explanations.a: Correct. The remaining functional nephrons hypertrophy and compensate for damaged ones, masking the disease until severe damage has occurred.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While kidneys are internal organs, the 'silent' label refers to the lack of early symptoms, not the inability to feel pain.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Kidney disease can affect people of any age, though risk increases over 60.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Kidney disease does eventually cause symptoms such as high blood pressure, oedema, blood in urine and fatigue.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the urinary system's structure help protect the kidneys from UTI-causing bacteria?

options.text: The system prevents backflow of urine from the bladder to the kidneys, so most infections are restricted to the bladder
The kidneys produce antibiotics that kill bacteria before they arrive
The ureters are too narrow for bacteria to pass through
The renal capsule is impermeable to all microorganisms

explanations.a: Correct. The urinary system has mechanisms that prevent urine from flowing backward from the bladder to the kidneys, keeping most bacterial infections localised to the lower urinary tract.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The kidneys do not produce antibiotics. Antibiotics are prescribed externally to treat UTIs.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While the ureters are narrow, the main protective mechanism is the prevention of urine backflow.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The renal capsule is a protective layer but does not specifically prevent bacterial entry from the urinary tract.

toLevel3.stem: Why does chronic kidney disease often lead to high blood pressure?

options.text: Because damaged kidneys cannot filter waste or regulate fluid levels properly, causing fluid retention that increases blood volume and pressure
Because the kidneys produce adrenaline when they are damaged
Because kidney disease causes the heart to beat faster
Because urea directly raises blood pressure

explanations.a: Correct. When kidneys lose function, they cannot adequately filter waste or maintain fluid balance. Excess fluid builds up in the blood, increasing blood volume and therefore blood pressure.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands, not the kidneys themselves. Kidney disease does not cause excess adrenaline production.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While high blood pressure can affect heart rate, the primary mechanism is fluid retention due to impaired kidney function.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While urea accumulation is harmful, the blood pressure increase is primarily due to fluid and salt retention.

toLevel3.stem: How do UTI treatments such as alkalinisers help ease symptoms?

options.text: They neutralise the acidity of urine, reducing the burning sensation during urination
They kill the bacteria causing the infection
They increase urine volume to flush out bacteria
They strengthen the walls of the urethra

explanations.a: Correct. Alkalinisers reduce urine acidity, which helps ease the burning pain. The actual bacterial infection is treated with prescribed antibiotics.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Alkalinisers do not kill bacteria. Antibiotics are needed to clear the bacterial infection.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While drinking water helps flush bacteria, alkalinisers specifically target urine acidity to reduce pain.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Alkalinisers do not affect the structure of the urethra.

toLevel3.stem: Why might puffiness in the legs and ankles be a symptom of kidney disease?

options.text: Because the kidneys can no longer regulate fluid levels, causing excess fluid to accumulate in tissues
Because kidney disease causes muscles in the legs to swell
Because bacteria from the kidneys travel to the legs
Because the kidneys produce too much ADH

explanations.a: Correct. When kidneys cannot properly filter blood and regulate fluid, excess water and salts are retained, leading to oedema (fluid accumulation in tissues), particularly in the lower limbs.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The swelling is due to fluid retention in tissues, not muscle swelling.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Kidney disease symptoms in the legs are caused by fluid retention, not bacterial spread.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While ADH regulation may be affected, the oedema is primarily due to the kidneys' inability to excrete excess fluid.

toLevel3.stem: What is the difference between acute and chronic kidney failure?

options.text: Acute kidney failure occurs suddenly while chronic kidney failure develops gradually over years
Acute kidney failure is permanent while chronic kidney failure is temporary
Acute kidney failure affects only one kidney; chronic affects both
Acute kidney failure is caused by bacteria; chronic is caused by viruses

explanations.a: Correct. Acute kidney failure occurs suddenly, often due to an accident or sudden event. Chronic kidney failure is a progressive condition that develops over months or years.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Acute kidney failure can sometimes be reversed if treated quickly, while chronic kidney failure involves permanent progressive damage.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Both acute and chronic kidney failure can affect one or both kidneys depending on the cause.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Neither type is specifically caused by viruses. Risk factors for chronic kidney disease include diabetes, high blood pressure and family history.

toLevel3.stem: UTIs are life-threatening conditions that require hospitalisation.

distractor.explanation: While UTIs are uncomfortable, they are generally not life-threatening. Symptoms can be eased by drinking water and taking alkalinisers, and the infection is cleared with prescribed antibiotics.

toLevel3.stem: Kidney disease is called a 'silent disease' because up to {{blank:1}}% of kidney function can be lost before symptoms appear.
UTI symptoms can be eased by drinking water and taking an {{blank:1}} to neutralise urine, while {{blank:2}} are prescribed to clear the bacterial infection.
Chronic kidney disease may eventually require {{blank:1}} to artificially filter the blood or a kidney {{blank:2}}.

toLevel4.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has blood tests showing elevated urea levels and high blood pressure. Explain the link between these symptoms.

options.text: Damaged nephrons cannot filter urea from blood (causing elevated urea) or regulate fluid volume (causing fluid retention and high blood pressure)
Elevated urea directly increases heart rate, raising blood pressure
High blood pressure causes urea to leak back from urine into the blood
The symptoms are unrelated and occur independently

explanations.a: Correct. Both symptoms trace back to nephron damage. Reduced filtration means urea accumulates in blood, and impaired fluid regulation causes water and salt retention, increasing blood volume and pressure.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Urea does not directly increase heart rate. The high blood pressure is caused by fluid retention due to impaired kidney function.
explanations.c: Incorrect. High blood pressure does not cause urea to move from urine back into blood. Both symptoms result from the same underlying kidney damage.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Both symptoms share the same cause: loss of nephron function in the kidneys.

toLevel4.stem: A female patient presents with burning pain during urination, frequent urge to urinate and cloudy urine. What is the most likely diagnosis and why?

options.text: A UTI, because these are classic symptoms of bacterial infection in the lower urinary tract and females are at higher risk
Chronic kidney disease, because burning pain indicates nephron damage
Diabetes, because frequent urination is a symptom of high blood glucose
Dehydration, because concentrated urine causes burning

explanations.a: Correct. Burning pain, frequent urination with small volume and cloudy/smelly urine are classic UTI symptoms. The shorter female urethra (4 cm) makes women 14 times more likely to develop UTIs.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Chronic kidney disease typically presents with high blood pressure, oedema and fatigue, not burning during urination.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While diabetes can cause frequent urination, the combination of burning pain and cloudy urine points to a UTI.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Dehydration causes dark, concentrated urine but not typically burning pain or cloudy urine.

toLevel4.stem: A patient has lost 85% of kidney function but shows no symptoms. What explains this?

options.text: The remaining functional nephrons hypertrophy and compensate for the damaged ones, maintaining adequate filtration
The liver takes over the kidney's filtration function
The patient is not producing any waste products
The bladder stores waste that would normally be filtered

explanations.a: Correct. Remaining healthy nephrons increase in size and workload to compensate for damaged ones. This is why kidney disease can progress silently until approximately 90% of function is lost.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The liver performs different functions (e.g. producing urea from ammonia) but cannot filter blood like the kidneys.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The body continuously produces metabolic waste. The remaining nephrons are processing the waste more intensively.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The bladder stores urine, not unfiltered waste. Filtration occurs in the kidneys.

toLevel4.stem: A doctor recommends that a patient with recurrent UTIs drink plenty of water. How does this help?

options.text: Increased water intake produces more urine, which helps flush bacteria out of the urinary tract
Water kills bacteria directly by diluting them
Water prevents bacteria from entering through the urethra
Water strengthens the immune system to fight infection

explanations.a: Correct. Drinking water increases urine production, which physically flushes bacteria from the urethra and bladder, reducing the bacterial load.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Dilution does not kill bacteria. The benefit comes from flushing them out through increased urine flow.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Water does not create a physical barrier at the urethra. It helps by increasing urine flow to remove bacteria already present.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While hydration is important for overall health, the primary benefit for UTIs is mechanical flushing of bacteria.

toLevel4.stem: A patient with diabetes and high blood pressure is told they are at high risk of chronic kidney disease. Why do these conditions increase kidney disease risk?

options.text: Both conditions damage the blood vessels in the kidneys, including the glomerular capillaries, reducing filtration capacity over time
Both conditions cause bacteria to enter the kidney
Both conditions increase ADH release, overworking the collecting duct
Both conditions reduce blood flow to the kidneys, stopping filtration immediately

explanations.a: Correct. High blood glucose (diabetes) and high blood pressure both damage the delicate capillaries in the kidneys, including the glomeruli, progressively impairing filtration and leading to nephron loss.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Diabetes and high blood pressure do not introduce bacteria. UTIs are caused by bacteria entering the urethra.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While ADH regulation may be affected, the primary mechanism of kidney damage is vascular damage from sustained high glucose and pressure.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Blood flow is not stopped immediately. The damage is progressive, occurring over years.

toLevel4.stem: Why might a patient with kidney disease show protein in their urine?

options.text: Damaged glomerular capillaries allow proteins to pass into the filtrate, and they are excreted in urine
The proximal tubule secretes proteins into the filtrate
The collecting duct produces proteins as a defence mechanism
Proteins are added to urine in the bladder

explanations.a: Correct. In healthy kidneys, proteins are too large to pass through the glomerular filter. When the glomerular capillaries are damaged by kidney disease, proteins leak into the filtrate and appear in urine (proteinuria).
explanations.b: Incorrect. The proximal tubule reabsorbs substances; it does not secrete proteins.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The collecting duct does not produce proteins.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The bladder stores urine but does not add proteins to it.

toLevel4.stem: Why does dialysis become necessary for patients with severe chronic kidney disease?

options.text: Because the kidneys can no longer adequately filter waste or regulate fluid, so a machine must perform these functions externally
Because dialysis replaces the hormones normally produced by the kidney
Because dialysis cures kidney disease by regenerating nephrons
Because dialysis increases blood pressure to improve filtration

explanations.a: Correct. When kidney function falls below the level needed to sustain life, dialysis artificially filters waste and excess fluid from the blood, substituting for the kidneys' lost function.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Dialysis primarily filters blood; it does not replace endocrine functions of the kidney.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Dialysis does not cure kidney disease or regenerate nephrons. It is a maintenance treatment.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Dialysis does not work by raising blood pressure. It mechanically filters the blood outside the body.

toLevel4.stem: In kidney disease, damaged {{blank:1}} allow proteins to leak into the filtrate, which then appear in the patient's urine.
Diabetes and {{blank:1}} are both risk factors for chronic kidney disease because they damage the blood vessels in the kidneys over time.
When kidney function is severely reduced, {{blank:1}} is used to artificially filter waste and excess fluid from the blood.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why chronic kidney disease often goes undetected until severe damage has occurred, while UTIs are typically detected early.

options.text: Remaining nephrons compensate for damaged ones in kidney disease, masking symptoms; UTIs cause immediate localised symptoms like pain and burning that prompt patients to seek help
Kidney disease has no symptoms at any stage; UTIs always cause hospitalisation
Both conditions are detected equally early through routine blood tests
UTIs damage more nephrons than kidney disease, causing more noticeable symptoms

explanations.a: Correct. Kidney disease progresses silently because nephron compensation masks the decline. UTIs produce obvious symptoms (burning, frequent urination, cloudy urine) that patients notice immediately, leading to early detection.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Kidney disease does eventually produce symptoms (high blood pressure, oedema), just very late. UTIs are uncomfortable but rarely require hospitalisation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. UTIs are usually detected through symptoms before blood tests, while kidney disease often requires screening to detect early.
explanations.d: Incorrect. UTIs typically affect the lower urinary tract and do not damage nephrons.

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'Since UTIs are not life-threatening, they do not need to be treated.' Evaluate this claim.

options.text: It is flawed because untreated UTIs can spread from the bladder to the kidneys, potentially causing serious kidney infection and damage
It is correct because UTIs always resolve on their own
It is correct because antibiotics are only needed for kidney disease
It is flawed because UTIs are always life-threatening

explanations.a: Correct. While most UTIs are restricted to the bladder and are not life-threatening, untreated infections can ascend to the kidneys, causing pyelonephritis (kidney infection), which can lead to serious complications.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While mild UTIs may sometimes resolve, antibiotics are recommended to prevent the infection from worsening or spreading.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Antibiotics are the standard treatment for UTIs to clear the bacterial infection.
explanations.d: Incorrect. UTIs are generally not life-threatening, but the claim is still flawed because they should be treated to prevent complications.

toLevel5.stem: Compare how kidney disease and UTIs affect the excretory system differently.

options.text: Kidney disease progressively destroys nephron function, reducing filtration and fluid regulation; UTIs cause localised bacterial infection in the lower urinary tract without directly damaging nephrons
Both conditions destroy nephrons equally
UTIs affect filtration while kidney disease affects only the bladder
Kidney disease is caused by bacteria while UTIs are caused by nephron loss

explanations.a: Correct. Kidney disease directly impairs nephron function, affecting the kidney's ability to filter blood. UTIs involve bacterial infection primarily in the urethra and bladder, which are downstream from the nephrons.
explanations.b: Incorrect. UTIs do not typically destroy nephrons. They affect the lower urinary tract.
explanations.c: Incorrect. UTIs affect the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder), not filtration. Kidney disease is what impairs filtration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. UTIs are caused by bacteria. Kidney disease has multiple causes including diabetes and high blood pressure.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether urethra length alone explains the difference in UTI rates between males and females.

options.text: It is the primary anatomical factor, but other factors such as proximity of the urethra to bacterial sources and hormonal differences may also contribute
Yes, urethra length is the only factor because it determines how far bacteria must travel
No, urethra length is irrelevant; the difference is entirely due to immune system differences
Yes, because males never develop UTIs

explanations.a: Correct. The shorter female urethra (4 cm vs 20 cm) is the primary anatomical factor, but additional factors like the proximity of the urethral opening to bacterial sources contribute to the 14-fold higher rate in women.
explanations.b: Incorrect. While urethra length is the most significant factor, it is not the only one. Anatomical proximity and other factors also play a role.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Urethra length is a significant factor. Immune differences alone do not explain the 14-fold difference in UTI rates.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Males can develop UTIs; they are just much less common due to the longer urethra.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why high blood pressure is both a symptom and a risk factor for chronic kidney disease.

options.text: High blood pressure damages kidney blood vessels (risk factor), and damaged kidneys retain fluid causing blood pressure to rise further (symptom), creating a damaging cycle
They are the same condition with different names
High blood pressure causes bacteria to enter the kidney
High blood pressure only occurs after kidney disease has fully developed

explanations.a: Correct. This creates a vicious cycle: sustained high blood pressure damages glomerular capillaries, reducing kidney function. Reduced kidney function causes fluid retention, further increasing blood pressure, which causes more kidney damage.
explanations.b: Incorrect. High blood pressure and kidney disease are distinct conditions, but they are interconnected in a damaging feedback cycle.
explanations.c: Incorrect. High blood pressure damages blood vessels, not introduces bacteria. Bacterial infection causes UTIs, not kidney disease.
explanations.d: Incorrect. High blood pressure can exist before and independently of kidney disease, and it is a known risk factor that contributes to kidney disease development.

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that dialysis is a permanent cure for kidney disease. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect, because dialysis is a maintenance treatment that artificially filters blood but does not regenerate damaged nephrons or restore kidney function
Correct, because dialysis permanently replaces all kidney functions
Correct, because dialysis stimulates the growth of new nephrons
Incorrect, because dialysis only treats UTIs, not kidney disease

explanations.a: Correct. Dialysis substitutes for lost filtration function but must be performed regularly (often several times per week). It does not cure the disease. Only a kidney transplant can restore function, and even that requires lifelong immunosuppression.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Dialysis does not replace all kidney functions. It filters blood but does not produce hormones like the kidneys do.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Nephrons cannot regenerate. Once lost, kidney tissue does not regrow.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Dialysis is specifically used for kidney disease, not UTIs.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how the symptoms of kidney disease (blood in urine, protein in urine, oedema) each relate to specific aspects of nephron damage.

options.text: Blood and protein in urine indicate damaged glomerular filtration barriers; oedema indicates impaired fluid regulation by the tubules and collecting ducts
All symptoms result from bacterial infection of the nephron
Blood in urine comes from the bladder; protein comes from the liver; oedema is unrelated
All symptoms are caused by excess ADH production

explanations.a: Correct. Damaged glomeruli allow blood cells and proteins to leak into the filtrate. Impaired tubule and collecting duct function means the kidney cannot properly regulate water and salt balance, causing fluid to accumulate as oedema.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Kidney disease is not caused by bacterial infection (that would be a UTI). These symptoms reflect progressive structural damage.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Blood and protein in urine from kidney disease originate from damaged glomeruli in the kidneys, not from the bladder or liver.
explanations.d: Incorrect. While ADH regulation may be affected, the symptoms listed are caused by structural damage to the nephrons.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the importance of regular screening for kidney disease in people with diabetes.

options.text: It is crucial because kidney disease is silent until severe, and early detection through urine and blood tests allows intervention before irreversible damage
It is unnecessary because diabetes does not affect the kidneys
It is only useful after symptoms appear
It is unnecessary because UTI testing is sufficient to detect kidney disease

explanations.a: Correct. Since diabetes damages kidney blood vessels and kidney disease can progress to 90% loss before symptoms appear, regular screening (e.g. checking for protein in urine, blood urea levels) enables early intervention to slow progression.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Diabetes is one of the most significant risk factors for chronic kidney disease.
explanations.c: Incorrect. By the time symptoms appear, extensive irreversible damage has typically occurred. The whole point of screening is early detection.
explanations.d: Incorrect. UTI tests detect bacterial infections, not chronic kidney disease. Different tests are needed.

toLevel5.stem: High blood pressure and kidney disease form a {{blank:1}} cycle: high blood pressure damages kidney blood vessels, and damaged kidneys retain fluid, further {{blank:2}} blood pressure.
Dialysis is a {{blank:1}} treatment that artificially filters blood but does not {{blank:2}} damaged nephrons.
